description: Where data comes from, why it matters, and how reliability, validity and bias affect what you can conclude.
content_html:
Where Does Data Come From?

Every statistical investigation needs data — but that data has to come from somewhere. The two fundamental categories are primary data and secondary data. Understanding the difference between them — and knowing the advantages and limitations of each — is essential when planning an investigation and when evaluating someone else’s research.

Primary Data

Primary data is collected first-hand, specifically for your investigation. The main methods include:

  • Experimental: The researcher controls conditions to test a cause-and-effect relationship. A laboratory experiment removes external influences (high level of control). A field experiment takes place in a natural setting, which improves realism but reduces control. A natural experiment observes what happens when conditions change for non-research reasons — for example, observing the effect of a new bus route on school attendance rates.
  • Simulation: Uses models (often computer-based) to generate data when real-world collection is impossible or unethical — for example, simulating traffic patterns or the spread of an infectious disease.
  • Questionnaire: A set of written questions completed by participants. Cheap and scalable, but dependent on honest responses.
  • Observation: Watching and recording behaviour directly. Can capture what people actually do rather than what they say they do, but observer presence can influence behaviour.

Primary data has a major advantage: it is collected specifically for your purpose, so it should measure exactly what you need. The disadvantage is that it takes time and resources to collect.

Secondary Data

Secondary data already exists. Sources include published statistical databases, government censuses, academic studies, media reports, and reference publications. In the UK, organisations such as the Office for National Statistics (ONS), NHS Digital, the Met Office, and the Department for Education all publish large, high-quality datasets that researchers can use without collecting any data themselves.

The advantages of secondary data are significant: it is fast to access, often covers large populations, and may span decades of historical records that no individual researcher could replicate. The ONS Census, for example, covers the entire UK population at ten-year intervals — a dataset of that scale is simply not achievable through primary collection for most researchers.

However, secondary data has limitations. It was collected for a different purpose, so it may not measure exactly what you need. Variable definitions may differ — what counts as “unemployed” changed in UK statistics several times between the 1970s and 1990s, making long-run comparisons tricky. You also need to acknowledge the source of any secondary data you use, as the specification requires.

Key Fact

Secondary data: advantages — fast to access, large sample sizes, historical depth. Limitations — may not measure exactly what you need, variable definitions may have changed, source must be acknowledged and its quality assessed.

Census vs Sample

A census collects data from every member of the population. The UK Census, conducted every ten years, aims to record information about every household. A census gives complete data with no sampling error, but it is expensive, time-consuming, and in some cases impossible (not every person can be reached).

In contrast, sampling involves collecting data from a carefully chosen subset. Most practical investigations use samples. The challenge is making the sample representative enough that conclusions about the population are valid.

Reliability and Validity

These two words are used precisely in statistics and are often confused. Reliability is about consistency: does the measurement give the same result every time you use it? Validity is about accuracy of purpose: does the measurement capture the thing you actually want to know about?

A useful way to see the difference: imagine a bathroom scale that always reads 3 kg too heavy. It is reliable — it gives a consistent reading every time — but it is not valid for measuring your true weight. Conversely, asking students “How healthy do you feel?” on a scale of 1–10 might produce variable answers from the same student on different days (poor reliability) and may not accurately capture their clinical health status (poor validity).

Students frequently write “the data is reliable and valid” as if the two words mean the same thing, or they use one when they mean the other. In the exam, using these terms imprecisely will cost marks.

If a question asks about reliability, focus on: would repeated measurements give the same result? If it asks about validity, focus on: does the measurement actually capture what you want to measure? A questionnaire asking about income to proxy for social class is valid if income correlates well with social class — but only reliable if the same person answers the same question consistently across administrations.

Bias and Sensitivity

Bias is a systematic error — it pushes results in one direction rather than producing random noise. Bias can arise from: the way a sample is selected (sampling bias), the way questions are worded (response bias), or the sensitivity of the topic being researched.

Sensitive topics — income, health, political views, personal relationships — are particularly prone to response bias. People may give socially desirable answers rather than honest ones, or they may refuse to answer at all (non-response bias). When the people who refuse to answer share a characteristic relevant to the investigation, this creates a systematic distortion in the results.

Level of Control and Minimising Data Distortion (Higher)

In a controlled experiment, the researcher manipulates one variable (the explanatory variable) and keeps all others constant, so that any change in the response variable can be attributed to the manipulation. The level of control refers to how completely the investigator can hold other variables constant.

High control (laboratory experiments) makes causation easier to claim but may reduce ecological validity — the results may not apply to real-world settings. Low control (natural experiments, observational studies) reflects real-world conditions better but makes it harder to isolate cause and effect because other variables are free to vary.

Extraneous variables — variables that influence the response variable but are not the focus of the investigation — must be identified and managed. Techniques include controlling them directly (holding them constant across all participants), including a control group (a group that receives no treatment, against which the experimental group is compared), and randomisation (randomly assigning participants to groups so that extraneous variables are spread evenly).

Key Fact

Reliability = consistency across repeated measurements. Validity = the measurement captures what it is supposed to measure. A data source can be one without the other.

The specification explicitly states that secondary data sources should be acknowledged. In practice, this means recording where the data came from, when it was collected or published, and who collected it. This matters for two reasons.

First, it allows the reader to check the original source and assess its quality. A statistic from a government body such as the ONS is more likely to be reliable than one from a company’s own press release. Second, without acknowledgement, using someone else’s data without credit is a form of academic misconduct. In professional statistical work and in your investigation write-up, always note the source.
exam_tip_html: On ‘Explain’ questions asking you to evaluate a data source, always link reliability and validity to the specific method described in the question. Saying “questionnaires are not always reliable” earns no marks — you need to say why this specific questionnaire on this specific topic may produce inconsistent or inaccurate results. Sensitivity of the topic is often the key reason: if the topic is sensitive (e.g. income, health), responses are more likely to be incomplete or biased. On ‘Discuss’ questions, always present both advantages and limitations before reaching a judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Primary data is collected first-hand for the specific investigation; secondary data already exists and was collected by someone else for a different purpose — both have advantages and limitations that must be evaluated in context.
  • Reliability means consistency of measurement across repeated applications; validity means the measurement captures the construct it is supposed to measure — these are different properties and a measure can have one without the other.
  • Bias arises when systematic errors push results in one direction; sensitivity of the topic is a common source of response bias and non-response, which distorts conclusions if not managed proactively.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of secondary data?
A) A student conducts a survey of her classmates' screen time.
B) A researcher observes shoppers in a supermarket and records their behaviour.
C) A student downloads data about UK birth rates from the Office for National Statistics website.
D) A science class measures the reaction times of 30 volunteers.
practice_questions.marks: C [1 mark] — Data downloaded from the ONS was collected by someone else for a different purpose and already exists, making it secondary data.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher measures the resting heart rate of a sample of students on Monday, then measures the same students again on Wednesday under identical conditions, and gets almost the same values.
State whether this suggests the measurement is reliable, valid, or both. Give a reason for your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Reliable [1 mark] because the measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions [1 mark].
Note: this does not tell us about validity — it could still be an inaccurate proxy for cardiovascular health.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using secondary data from a government census for a statistical investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each point clearly stated, up to 3 marks.
Advantage: the census covers the entire population, giving a very large dataset with no sampling error [1].
Disadvantage (any one of the following):
- The data was collected for a different purpose, so it may not measure exactly what the current investigation needs [1].
- Variable definitions may have changed between census years, making long-run comparisons unreliable [1].
- The census is conducted infrequently (every ten years), so it may not reflect current conditions [1].

practice_questions.text:
A school wants to investigate whether students who eat a hot lunch report higher energy levels in afternoon lessons than those who eat a packed lunch. A teacher designs a questionnaire where students rate their energy level on a scale of 1 to 10.
Explain one reason why this measurement method may lack validity for this investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Validity issue identified and clearly linked to why the measurement does not capture what is being studied.
- A self-rated energy score on a 1-10 scale may not validly measure actual energy levels [1] because students may interpret ‘energy’ differently (physical tiredness vs motivation vs alertness), so the scale does not consistently capture the same construct across participants [1].
- The measurement is susceptible to demand characteristics [1]: students may give a higher score if they know the teacher believes hot lunches are better, not because their energy is actually higher [1].
Secure: Validity issue identified with partial development.
Developing: Raises reliability or bias without correctly addressing validity.
Emerging: States the questionnaire is ‘not accurate’ without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
A university researcher wants to investigate the link between social media use and self-reported wellbeing in teenagers. She plans to use secondary data from a published government survey.
Suggest and justify two limitations of using this secondary data for her investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each limitation and 1 mark for a justification that links to why it matters for this specific investigation, up to 5 marks.
Mastering: Two distinct limitations, each justified with reference to the specific investigation.
- The government survey may not have measured social media use and wellbeing in the same way the researcher defines them [1], so the variables in the secondary data may not align with her research question, reducing validity [1].
- The secondary data was collected at a single point in time or over a period that may not reflect current teenage social media habits [1], which have changed rapidly, reducing the relevance of the conclusions [1].
- The survey may not include all teenagers (not a census) or may have a non-representative sample [1], which would limit how far the conclusions can be generalised [1].
Secure: Two limitations identified, one justified.
Developing: One limitation identified and justified.
Emerging: Names 'secondary data' as a limitation without explaining why.

practice_questions.text:
A news headline claims: 'New study shows people who drink coffee live longer — researchers surveyed 500 coffee drinkers and 500 non-drinkers.'
Discuss the reliability and validity of the conclusions this study can support.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion covering reliability, validity, and potential limitations of the study design.
Mastering: Both reliability and validity addressed with reference to the study design, plus a judgement.
- Reliability concern: a survey measures self-reported coffee consumption, which may vary over time and be inconsistently recalled [1+1].
- Validity concern: the survey measures longevity only in the sample at the point of collection; tracking who lives longest requires a longitudinal study over many years [1+1].
- Confounding/bias: heavy coffee drinkers might share other lifestyle characteristics (higher income, better access to healthcare) that actually explain longevity differences [1+1].
- Judgement: the conclusions are not reliable or valid enough to claim a causal link; the study can only suggest an association that warrants further investigation [1].
Secure: Two of the three threads (reliability, validity, confounding) with partial development.
Developing: One thread with limited development.
Emerging: Describes what the study does without evaluating it.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following correctly defines reliability in statistics?
options: The extent to which a measurement captures what it is supposed to measure
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated
The extent to which the sample represents the population
The extent to which data is free from response bias

knowledge_checks.q: A researcher uses ONS population data for her investigation into UK birth trends. What type of data is this?
options: Primary data collected by field experiment
Secondary data from a reference publication

knowledge_checks.q: Data collected directly by the researcher for the specific purpose of the current investigation is called _____ data.
A bathroom scale that always reads 3 kg too heavy is _____ but not valid.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: A data collection that includes every member of the population
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated
A systematic distortion that pushes results consistently in one direction

flashcard_questions.a: Data collected first-hand by the researcher for the specific purpose of their investigation.
Data that already exists, collected by someone else for a different purpose.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two UK organisations that publish secondary statistical data.
flashcard_questions.a: The Office for National Statistics (ONS) and NHS Digital.
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
The extent to which a measurement actually captures what it is supposed to measure.

flashcard_questions.q: A scale always reads 3 kg heavy. Is it reliable, valid, neither, or both?
flashcard_questions.a: Reliable but not valid — consistent but inaccurate.

flashcard_questions.q: What is bias in a statistical context?
flashcard_questions.a: A systematic distortion that consistently pushes results in one direction away from the true value.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must sources of secondary data be acknowledged?
flashcard_questions.a: So readers can assess quality and to credit the original collectors.
A data collection that includes every member of the population of interest.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of a laboratory experiment over a field experiment.
flashcard_questions.a: Higher level of control, making it easier to isolate cause and effect.

glossary_terms.definition: Data collected directly by the researcher for the specific purpose of the current investigation.
Data that already exists, having been collected by someone else for a different purpose.
A data collection that includes every member of the population of interest.
Selecting a subset of the population to collect data from, with the aim of drawing conclusions about the whole population.
The extent to which a measurement gives consistent results when repeated under the same conditions.
The extent to which a measurement actually measures what it is supposed to measure.
A systematic distortion in data or results that causes them to consistently differ from the true value in a particular direction.
